title: Teaching: collar and clearing the C-spine
stem: Teaching room. A junior doctor asks you how to size and apply a cervical collar, and how to decide whether a patient's neck can be cleared without imaging. Teach them, then work through two quick cases with them.
notes:
Checked against the Canadian C-spine Rule (Stiell 2001, 2003), NEXUS (Hoffman 2000), NICE NG41 (Spinal injury: assessment and initial management, 2016) and NICE NG232 (head injury imaging), and the Faculty of Pre-Hospital Care consensus on spinal motion restriction (2018).

Collar: measure from the angle of the jaw to the top of the trapezius with your fingers, set or choose the collar to that height (measured from the sizing post to the bottom of the rigid plastic), slide the back under the neck while someone holds manual in-line stabilisation, bring the front up under the chin, fasten, and check the fit. Blocks and tape complete immobilisation. Current consensus favours minimal handling and 'spinal motion restriction': collars can raise ICP, cause pressure sores and aspiration, and are no longer routine in every patient (for example, the self-extricating, ambulant patient). Your notes' indications and complications are correct; they present collars as universal, which current guidance does not.

Clearance: in an alert (GCS 15), stable, sober adult, apply the Canadian C-spine Rule. High risk (age 65 or over, dangerous mechanism, or paraesthesia in the limbs) → image. Otherwise, any low-risk factor (simple rear-end collision, sitting up in the ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed onset of neck pain, no midline tenderness) allows range-of-motion testing: can rotate 45° left and right → cleared. NEXUS is an alternative (no midline tenderness, no intoxication, normal alertness, no focal deficit, no painful distracting injury). CT is the first-line imaging in adults (NICE). Your notes match this.

steps.label: Talk to Dr Lau
steps.hint: Introduce, set objectives, find out what they know.

turns.line: Thanks for this. I get nervous about necks.

opts.t: Today: fit a collar correctly, and use the Canadian C-spine Rule on two cases. What do you know so far?
opts.r: I know NEXUS a bit. Never fitted a collar.
opts.mark: Sets objectives and assesses prior knowledge

steps.label: Fit the collar (on the manikin)
steps.hint: In-line stabilisation, measure, size, apply, check, blocks and tape.

opts.t: Someone holds manual in-line stabilisation throughout
Measure with fingers from the angle of the jaw to the top of the trapezius
Set the collar to that height: sizing post to the bottom of the rigid plastic
opts.mark: Sizes the collar to the measurement

opts.t: Slide the back under the neck, bring the front up under the chin, fasten
Check the fit: chin in the chin piece, no gap, airway and pulses accessible
Add blocks and tape (head first, then chin)
Pull the collar on tight so it can't move
opts.r: Too tight obstructs venous return (raises ICP) and the airway.

steps.label: Two quick cases
steps.hint: Apply the Canadian C-spine Rule aloud with Dr Lau.

turns.line: Case 1: 35-year-old, rear-ended at a traffic light, walking at the scene, GCS 15, no midline tenderness, sitting up. Clear?

opts.t: No high-risk factor, low-risk factors present, so test rotation: 45° both ways → cleared, no imaging
opts.r: So the rotation test is the last step.
opts.mark: Applies the CCR correctly in a low-risk case

opts.t: CT for everyone in a car crash
opts.r: Isn't that a lot of radiation?

turns.line: Case 2: 72-year-old, fell from standing, neck pain, GCS 15. Clear?

opts.t: Age 65 or over is high risk → CT C-spine, no rotation test
opts.mark: Recognises a high-risk factor mandating imaging

opts.t: Ask her to rotate her neck — if she can, clear
You tell me the three CCR steps.
opts.r: High risk → image; low risk → test rotation; can rotate → clear.

opts.t: Just follow the flowchart on the wall.

qs.q: Which is a Canadian C-spine Rule high-risk factor?
wrong: A simple rear-end motor vehicle collision
Delayed onset of neck pain after the crash
Able to sit up in the emergency department

qs.q: Which is NOT a NEXUS criterion?
First-line C-spine imaging in an adult who needs it (NICE)?
A dangerous mechanism in the CCR includes…
wrong: Twisting the neck at the gym

qs.q: A harm of a tight collar?

badge.name: Neck Guard
badge.flavor: High risk → image. Low risk → rotate 45°. Can do → clear.

cards.q: Canadian C-spine Rule: which mandates imaging?
cards.why: Age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, or limb paraesthesia.

cards.q: The CCR rotation test requires turning the head…

options: Jaw angle to trapezius, in finger breadths
Chin to sternal notch, in finger breadths
The patient's height and weight on a chart
cards.why: Match that distance to the rigid part of the collar.

cards.q: First-line C-spine imaging in adults (NICE NG41)?
cards.why: CT is more sensitive and faster in adults.

cards.q: NEXUS requires which to be absent?
cards.why: NEXUS: no midline tenderness, no intoxication, normal alertness, no focal deficit, no painful distracting injury.

options: Motion restriction; collars not routine for all
Rigid collar and long board for every trauma patient
Soft collar for all patients until X-rays are done
No precautions unless a deficit is present
cards.why: Collars have harms; the self-extricating, ambulant patient may not need one.
